title: Random Forests
hook: Grow hundreds of slightly different decision trees and average their votes - the crowd is smarter than any individual tree, and much harder to overfit.
key_points: Each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample (random subset of rows with replacement).
At each split, only a random subset of features is considered - this decorrelates the trees.
Predictions are made by majority vote (classification) or averaging (regression).
Out-of-bag samples provide a free validation estimate without a separate holdout set.
A strong, low-maintenance baseline for tabular data with minimal tuning required.
content_html: A random forest is an ensemble of decision trees, each grown on a slightly different random sample of the data and allowed to look at only a random subset of features at each split. When predicting, the trees vote and the majority wins.
extra_html:
How it works

Leo Breiman introduced the method in 2001. The two sources of randomness - bootstrap sampling of rows and random feature subsets at each split - keep the trees from being correlated with each other. Correlated errors would cancel less effectively; uncorrelated ones largely cancel out when averaged, which is why the ensemble does far better than any individual tree. The algorithm also tracks which samples each tree did not see during training (out-of-bag samples), using them as a built-in validation set to estimate generalization error.

Why it matters

Random forests remain a go-to first model for tabular data because they are robust, resistant to overfitting, and require little hyperparameter tuning. They also naturally provide feature importance scores. Breiman's original paper is still worth reading for the theoretical intuition behind why averaging decorrelated trees is so effective.
